The complete Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks collects the journals Hawthorne kept on his travels through France and Italy. The record opens in January 1858 with a cold pre-dawn departure from London. The family crosses to Paris by way of Folkestone and Boulogne, frost clouding the carriage windows.

From Paris the notebooks move on into Italy, its cities, churches, and galleries. Hawthorne writes as a traveller first and a famous author second, setting down weather, roads, food, and art. The two volumes together form his fullest travel record from his European years.
paul-clifford-complete:
Edward Bulwer-Lytton's Paul Clifford is a novel with a highwayman for its hero, and the author used his prefaces to explain why. In the preface to the 1840 edition he says the book attacks two evils: prison discipline that corrupts boys, and a hanging code that then destroys the men those boys become.

The complete text follows Paul from boyhood through crime to the shadow of the gallows at Newgate. Bulwer-Lytton also mocks fashionable vice by showing it as the mirror of vulgar vice. Part adventure, part reform tract, the novel argues that society manufactures the criminals it punishes.
pelham-complete:
Edward Bulwer Lytton's Pelham tells its story in the hero's own voice. Henry Pelham is the only child of a younger son of an old earl and a dowerless Scotch peer's daughter. The complete novel opens with his cheerful account of family ruin: bailiffs in the house, his mother's diamonds pawned, and a lucky legacy spent on a Turkish tent party.

Pelham grows from dandy to politician inside this glittering world. The book mixes memoir, satire, and a murder mystery, and it made Lytton's name. Its wit runs on the gap between what society shows and what it hides.
pelle-the-conqueror-complete: The hosted sample stops at the front matter of Pelle the Conqueror, the title page and contents, with no chapter text visible. The title page names Martin Andersen Nexø as the author and Jessie Muir and Bernard Miall as translators from the Danish. The contents divide the complete novel into great stages of a working boy's life, beginning with Boyhood and Apprenticeship, each part broken into many numbered chapters.
pepys-diary-complete:
Samuel Pepys, a rising naval official in London, kept a private diary from 1660 to 1669. He wrote in shorthand, for his eyes only, and stopped when he feared for his sight. The full text is the most famous diary in English.

Pepys records the Great Plague, the Great Fire, wars, plays, and court gossip. He also notes his meals, his music, his quarrels, and his rise at the Navy Office. Nothing is too grand or too small for his pen. The result is Restoration London, lived day by day, in unmatched detail. He also kept it hidden, writing of his faults as freely as his triumphs.
petty-troubles-of-married-life-complete:
Balzac's Petty Troubles of Married Life, in the complete edition, opens by asking whether its first trouble is petty or profound. A child, a husband exclaims at the baptism of his eleventh, costs terribly dear. Balzac answers that every petty trouble is a blessing for someone.

He invents Caroline, type of all wives, and Adolphe, her husband, lawyer, captain, engineer, or rich proprietor's son. Around their marriage he arranges dozens of small vexations: money, mothers-in-law, vanity, and boredom. The comedy is systematic, almost a science of wedlock, and the wit keeps cutting because the observations stay true.
pg-edition-of-netherlands-series-complet:
John Lothrop Motley's History of the Netherlands, in this complete Project Gutenberg edition, covers 1555 to 1623 in three works. The Rise of the Dutch Republic, the History of the United Netherlands, and the Life and Death of John of Barneveld stand together here, with Oliver Wendell Holmes's memoir of Motley.

Motley's preface calls the rise of the Dutch Republic one of the leading events of modern times, an organized protest without which later centuries change entirely. An editor's note adds that Motley served as American minister to Austria and England. The series made him the great English-language historian of Dutch liberty.
photos-and-maps-of-trinity-atomic-test-s:
Photos and Maps of Trinity (Atomic Test) Site is a picture file issued by the Public Affairs Office of the U.S. Army's White Sands Missile Range. The text is a list of the images themselves, each with a caption. It is the documentary record of the first atomic bomb test in the New Mexico desert in 1945, preserved as a simple set of pictures and maps.

The captions name the base camp, the blast at ten seconds, and the crater where Oppenheimer and Groves examine a tower piling. Others show the gadget being lifted into its hundred-foot tower, Norris Bradbury with the device, the unloading of Jumbo, and the McDonald-Schmidt ranch house where the plutonium core was assembled. Maps of the roads and the visitors' site close the set.
pierre-and-his-people-tales-of-the-far-n:
Gilbert Parker's tales of the Canadian far north are gathered here in a complete five-volume set, built around Pretty Pierre and the people of the prairie and frontier country. Parker says most of his novels and stories grew from incidents and characters he knew, heard of closely, or found in history.

The volumes hold nineteen stories, from The Patrol of the Cypress Hills and God's Garrison to Shon McGann's Tobogan Ride, The Tall Master, and A Sanctuary of the Plains. Mounted Police, Hudson's Bay men, half-breeds, outlaws, and wanderers fill the pages. Read together, the tales form Parker's full picture of a hard northern world and the mixed peoples who lived in it.
pierrette:
Balzac dedicated Pierrette to Anna Hanska, calling its story full of melancholy and warning that sorrows may one day need her gentle hands. Katharine Prescott Wormeley translated the novel, which belongs to his great picture of French manners and morals.

The story opens at dawn on an October day in 1827, in a small square of Lower Provins. A young fellow of about sixteen, dressed like a working boy, studies the quiet houses while the mills along the river are already turning. Balzac lingers on linden trees, grape vines, and rose-covered fronts, painting the peaceful, matter-of-fact life of the bourgeoisie before the sad history of Pierrette begins.
podcast-joerogan-6HZL9fXWgTE:
Two consumer scares share one segment of the Joe Rogan Experience: asbestos found in baby powder, and a protective coating for produce linked to Bill Gates. Rogan treats them as one story about trust: what companies put on our bodies and food, and who checks.

The talk moves through lawsuits over talc powder and the debate over how the coating works and whether it is safe. Rogan asks why such products reach shelves before the public hears of risks. The segment is part health news, part suspicion of big firms, and it shows the show's habit of worrying out loud over everyday products.
poems-by-emily-dickinson-three-series-co:
Emily Dickinson's complete early poems appear here in one volume, edited by two of her friends, Mabel Loomis Todd and Thomas Wentworth Higginson. Their long preface calls her work the poetry of the portfolio, verse written with no thought of publication at all. Dickinson, born in Amherst in 1830 and dead there in 1886. Lived as a recluse who rarely left her father's grounds and hid her mind from all but a few friends.

The preface admits she was persuaded to print only three or four poems in her lifetime. Yet wrote in great abundance, revising single words many times to please her own exacting ear. All three series stand together in this edition, hundreds of lyrics on death, nature, faith, and thought. It is the fullest early presentation of the poet who reshaped American poetry from a bedroom desk.
poems-on-serious-and-sacred-subjects-pri:
Chichester readers in 1818 could not buy this volume in a shop. Because its title page announces that the poems were printed only as private tokens of regard for the particular friends of the author, at the private press of W. Mason. The author goes unnamed on the title page. A Latin tag from Milton's circle and its English rendering set the theme: a Christian's kindness ends not in the tomb.

The first poem, an epistle to a lady on the fear of death dated 1768. Asks why dread of the grave grips the thoughtless young and the reflecting old, the feeble and the strong alike. Guilt may explain fear in a pirate, the poem argues, but the guiltless tremble too. Serious and sacred subjects fill the book: devotional meditations meant for a circle of friends, preserved now beyond the circle they were made for.
prince-zilah-complete:
Jules Claretie wrote Prince Zilah, presented complete here with a preface by the Comte d'Haussonville of the French Academy. A biographical sketch introduces the author: Arsène Arnaud Claretie, born at Limoges in December 1840. A journalist who wrote everything, entered the Academy in 1888, ran the Comédie-Française, and defended Dreyfus in 1899.

The novel itself, a romance of Parisian high life, turns on Prince Andras Zilah, a Hungarian magnate exiled by politics. His marriage to Marsa, a woman with a past that a blackmailer can weaponize. Paris salons, duels of honor, and gypsy music carry Claretie's melodrama, which France read as a faithful mirror of its fashionable world. The complete edition, life and work together, shows why the Academy crowned its author: nobody chronicled the Third Republic's drawing rooms with a busier or better-informed pen.
punch-or-the-london-charivari-volume-1-c:
Bound up whole, volume 1 of Punch gathers the London comic paper's first half year, from its launch in July 1841. An opening picture shows masked players around Mr. Punch, and the introduction promises a refuge for destitute wit and orphan jokes.

Department heads list the paper's wares: politics without party bias, fashions from Mrs. J. Punch, police reports, reviews, fine arts, music, and drama, with Mr. Punch himself doing the drama. The volume closes the paper's first season in one cover. Readers get the founding charter of a weekly that would run for a century and a half.
quotes-and-images-from-memoirs-of-marie-:
Quotes and Images from Marie Antoinette takes its passages from Madame Campan's memoirs of the Queen, Campan having served in her household. David Widger arranges the extracts alphabetically, and the Queen who emerges is proud, dutiful, and doomed, seen through a loyal servant's eyes.

Entries recall a man born solely to contradict. They recall the Duc d'Orléans called on to vote for the death of the King. They recall Hortense de Beauharnais brought to Campan as a child. "Better to die than to implicate anybody" stands among the lines. Other lines note rank carried to a high pitch. They note griefs that double the teller's own.
ragged-lady-complete:
Ragged Lady, by William Dean Howells, opens in Part One with the Landers on their first summer at Middlemount, lost on back roads in a carry-all. Mrs. Lander wants her husband to get out and ask the way to South Middlemount at a house by the pine woods, and she holds the reins to stop him driving on blind.

He jerks the reins anyway, then softens the insult by driving her up to the door so she can ask without climbing down, a favor given her age and bulk. The house they approach is raw and unfinished, banked with earth at its foundations, its boarding patchy and its front steps still just a block of wood.
rambles-in-the-mammoth-cave-during-the-y: Rambles in the Mammoth Cave, During the Year 1844, by a Visiter, names its author on the title page as Alexander Clark Bullitt. It was printed at Louisville, Kentucky, by Morton and Griswold in 1845. The pages shown are the errata and the publisher's advertisement. The advertisement offers the book to visitors calling for a work on the cave. It calls the book a succinct, instructive narrative of a visit. The cave is this wonder of wonders. A gentleman who had seen much of its recesses wrote it.
recollections-of-the-private-life-of-nap:
Constant, Napoleon's head valet, wrote this full account of his master's private life, here in Walter Clark's English version of 1895. A preface notes the work first appeared in 1830 and had never before been put into English. Clark got a scarce copy in Paris, added notes, and the publishers added pictures.

The preface promises Napoleon in undress: his faults and vices shown without reserve, but also his kind heart, vast mind, and great energy. It answers Prince Napoleon, who had attacked the book's truth in Napoleon and His Detractors. Clark finds no good reason to doubt that the account is genuine.
rhoda-fleming-complete:
George Meredith's novel of the Fleming sisters is printed complete here, in four books of contents. Book one opens with a Kentish family at Queen Anne's Farm. Chapter titles warn of the might of the money demon, bring the sisters together, and introduce Edward and Algernon, Mrs. Lovell, and Robert.

Book two moves between Rhoda and Robert, Wrexby Hall, and an assembly at the Pilot Inn, where Robert is smitten low. Book three promises a glimpse of poor villainies, Major Percy Waring, and a fearful temptation for Anthony Hackbut. Book four names its turns plainly: The Expiation, La Question d'Argent, Edward's Return, and Father and Son.
richard-carvel-complete:
Winston Churchill's historical novel Richard Carvel is printed complete here, its contents divided into volumes. The first chapters name Lionel Carvel of Carvel Hall and some memories of childhood. Richard, the narrator, is caught by the tide, suffers first for the Cause, and watches Grafton seek his chance.

Later lists carry him over the wall, under false colours, and into news from a far country. Mr. Allen shows his hand, South River and The Black Moll follow, and a man of destiny appears. London Town, a rescue, a conspiracy, and Drury Lane stand in the fifth volume's list. The tale joins a Maryland family's fortunes to the coming of revolution.
rob-roy-complete:
Sir Walter Scott's Rob Roy is printed complete here, opening with the advertisement to its first edition. A stanza from Wordsworth's Rob Roy's Grave heads the book: they should take who have the power, and they should keep who can. The advertisement jokes that its editor had promised, on publishing The Antiquary, to intrude no more in that capacity.

Like Benedict in the play, the editor said he would die a bachelor and lived to marry instead. He tells how a parcel of papers reached him through his publishers, holding the outlines of the narrative. A footnote in the 1829 edition owns the tale plainly: that communication was entirely imaginary.
routledge-s-manual-of-etiquette: Routledge's Manual of Etiquette, issued by George Routledge and Sons, gathers guides to polite conduct under one cover. The title page lists etiquette for ladies, etiquette for gentlemen, a ball-room companion, courtship and matrimony, how to dress well, how to carve, and toasts and sentiments. The contents for ladies run through introductions, letters of introduction, visiting and morning calls, cards, talk, notes of invitation, the promenade, and dress. Later sections cover morning and evening parties, the dinner table, the ball-room, and staying at a friend's house.
samantha-among-the-brethren-complete:
Marietta Holley, writing as Josiah Allen's Wife, wrote Samantha Among the Brethren, with pictures, dated 1890. The book is given to all women who work, trying to bring into dark lives the brightness and hope of a better country. In the preface Samantha watches her own story begin at home. Her companion Josiah Allen sees her walk up, take her inkstand off the mantelpiece. She carries it with a calm and majestic gait to the corner of the sitting-room table set aside for her writing.

Josiah asks what she is going to tackle now, and Samantha answers with dignity: the cause of eternal justice. Is there anything else, he asks, looking uneasy, a man who, she notes, realizes his shortcomings a good deal of the time. Yes, she says. She lays out in particular to tackle the Meeting House.
sandra-belloni-originally-emilia-in-engl: George Meredith wrote Sandra Belloni, and the contents divide the complete work into books of numbered chapters. Book 1 opens with The Poles Prelude, The Expedition by Moonlight, and Wilfrid's Diplomacy, then turns to Emilia's first trial in public and Emilia playing on the cornet. Later Book 1 chapters include Threats of a Crisis in the Government of Brookfield, The Rival Clubs, and The Ladies of Brookfield at School.
selected-stories-of-bret-harte:
Bret Harte's best-known tales of California mining camps fill this chosen set. Contents open with The Luck of Roaring Camp and The Outcasts of Poker Flat, the two stories that made his name. An opening essay frames the tales for new readers.

Other pieces include Miggles, Tennessee's Partner, Mliss, and Brown of Calaveras. Gold-rush camps supply gamblers, outcasts, rough men, and sudden acts of grace. Harte writes with warmth and irony about a raw new West. Readers meet the stories that taught the wider world how to picture California in the gold years.
serapis-complete:
Georg Ebers wrote this historical novel, here in English by Clara Bell, set in Alexandria in the year 391. Night lies over the city in the opening chapter, yet no true calm rests on its streets. Shops stay barred as if against thieves, and soldiers' steps ring through the dark.

Tension has gripped the city for weeks, as monks, pagans, and soldiers watch each other. An old man slips along a lane near the harbor called Kibotus, hugging the walls. Ebers builds a full picture of a great port city split by faith, on the edge of the clash that would end the cult of Serapis.
serge-panine-complete:
Georges Ohnet wrote this French novel, presented here in a series of great romances crowned by the French Academy. Gaston Boissier, the Academy's standing secretary, supplied a general opening essay for the series in 1905. The essay, signed by Robert Arnot, tells how the Maison Mazarin planned the set.

Editors sought the finest French romances since 1784 that had won the Academy's crown of merit. The Academy gave the plan its formal praise and support. Serge Panine stands among those honored works, offered to English readers as a window on the inner life of France at its literary height.
sketches-by-seymour-complete:
Robert Seymour's comic plates fill this set, issued in various forms about 1836 and here gathered complete from a Thomas Fry printing in London. An editor's note counts ninety plates, many engraved by H. Wallis from Seymour's sketches. The printed book merges five smaller volumes, with chapter order plainly muddled by the printer.

Everyday scenes open the fun: a sleeping fisherman, a morning lark, and the rapid march of intellect. The editor rates the engravings as the prize and the text as brief, pun-filled fun of its day. No text author is credited, though an Andrew Mullins piece may hide a pen name.
sylvia-s-lovers-complete:
Elizabeth Gaskell's Sylvia's Lovers, printed at London in M.DCCC.LXIII, or 1863, is a novel in three volumes set in the whaling town of Monkshaven on the north-eastern coast of England. A Tennyson motto about a voice behind the veil fronts the book, and an editor's note explains that the complete edition renumbers the later volumes' chapters in one sequence.

The contents of the first volume move from Monkshaven and a ship home from Greenland through the story of the press-gang and a sailor's funeral. Philip Hepburn enters early. Chapters on attraction and repulsion follow. The specksioneer and a refractory pupil come next. They build the triangle of Sylvia and her two men. One is her sailor lover. The other is the steady shopman who loves her in silence. A New Year's fete and partnership close the volume's list.
tales-and-novels-of-j-de-la-fontaine-com:
The Tales and Novels of J. de La Fontaine, in the complete English verse edition at hand, opens with a life of La Fontaine and a preface, then launches into Joconde. The table runs on through The Cudgelled and Contented Cuckold, The Husband Confessor, The Cobbler, and The Peasant and His Angry Lord.

Later titles sketch the whole merry, risky world of the tales. They give The Three Gossips' Wager and The Old Man's Calendar. They give The Magick Cup, The Falcon, and The Ephesian Matron. Belphegor, Hans Carvel's Ring, and The Mandrake follow. Many more stand behind them. La Fontaine retold Boccaccio and the old French fabliaux in witty verse, full of monks, jealous husbands, clever wives, and gallants caught in their own traps. A preface to the second book stands midway in the table.
tales-from-the-arabic-complete:
John Payne's Tales from the Arabic gathers stories in English dress. They come from the Breslau and Calcutta editions of The Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night. Those editions were printed in 1814 to 1818. The tales do not occur in the other printed texts of the work. The set, in three volumes, was issued in 1901 in a Delhi edition, and this record holds the first volume's contents in full.

The Breslau text opens with Asleep and Awake. The story of the lackpenny and the cook sits inside it. Tales of the Khalif Omar Ben Abdulaziz and the poets follow. A tale of Haroun Er Reshid and the woman of the Barmecides comes next. The Ten Viziers frames the history of King Azadbekht and his son, with inset tales on endeavor against ill fortune, patience, and haste. Payne's literal hand suits these rougher, less familiar nights.
tartuffe-or-the-hypocrite:
Jean Baptiste Poquelin Moliere wrote Tartuffe, or The Hypocrite, here rendered by Curtis Hidden Page with a life of the playwright set before the play. Moliere, born at Paris in January 1622, left law for the stage and spent his life acting and running companies.

The note recalls his death on February 17, 1673, hours after he fell ill while acting in The Imaginary Invalid. It also marks Les Precieuses Ridicules of 1659 as the work that lifted French comedy to satire of its own age. Tartuffe itself unmasks a false holy man who worms into a rich home. Readers get a sharp, famed attack on faked faith and blind trust.
telling-fortunes-by-tea-leaves-how-to-re:
Cicely Kent wrote Telling Fortunes by Tea Leaves, subtitled How to Read Your Fate in a Teacup, with twenty plates to show cup signs. Parts cover method, broad rules, hints for readers, tales of true calls made from leaves, and a full word list of signs.

Kent opens by noting a keen new hunt for light on psychic things in her day. Her book treats cup reading both as a game and as a graver study. Worked cups, paired signs, and the famed Nelros cup give hands-on guides. Readers get a calm, step-by-step path into a once-common parlor art, from brewing the cup to reading what the leaves leave behind.
the-1990-united-states-census-incomplete:
The 1990 United States Census, in this state-by-state form, gives counts for each state. Each page splits the count by sex and age. Broad age groups gain lines of their own. Alabama opens the set. Its total population is 4,040,587.

For Alabama, males count 1,936,162 and females count 2,104,425. The median age is 33.0 years. Children under eighteen make up 1,058,788 people. That is 26.2 percent of the state. Readers can trace how young or old each state was in 1990. They can see how its sexes balanced. They can set it next to its neighbors in the great national count of that year. The form suits quick checks of one state at a time.
the-adventures-of-ferdinand-count-fathom: Tobias Smollett wrote The Adventures of Ferdinand Count Fathom, here in a complete two-part printing with the author's own preface and an opening essay by G. H. Maynadier of Harvard University. Part one chapter heads trace Fathom's infancy, his start in army life, a rich patron, his mother's death, his schooling, and his first scams with a female partner in crime.
the-adventures-of-harry-richmond-complet: George Meredith wrote The Adventures of Harry Richmond. This complete printing heads the novel with a long chapter list. Early heads run from I Am a Subject of Contention first. Dipwell Farm and A Taste of Grandeur follow. A Free Life on the Road comes next. Janet Ilchester and Captain Bulsted then appear. The Great Fog and the Fire at Midnight stand midway. A sea voyage on the Priscilla follows. My Father Breathes, Moves, and Speaks closes the parts shown.
the-antiquary-complete: Bare contents pages are all that open this complete edition of The Antiquary by Sir Walter Scott, styled Baronet. Two picture plates are named, a title page and a frontispiece. Volume One is listed with an introduction and an editor's introduction, followed by chapters numbered in words from first to sixteenth and beyond. No chapter heads, dates, or story text appear in these opening pages.
the-arabian-nights-entertainments-comple:
Pickering and Chatto of London issued this Aldine Edition in 1890, with pictures by S. L. Wood and text from Dr. Jonathan Scott, in four volumes. The American small paper printing ran to only 500 copies. A publishers' preface says the set starts a planned series of reprints of standard English fiction.

Each book in the series, the preface promises, will be printed with art, pictured well, and set from a carefully chosen sound text. As for the tales themselves, the preface admits their exact source is unknown. In Arabic they are called The Thousand and One Nights, and the Caliph Haroon al Rusheed walks through many of them as if alive.
the-attache-or-sam-slick-in-england-comp:
Thomas Chandler Haliburton sends Sam Slick into England in this complete Attaché. A motto stands at the head, with Slick's own warning in Slickville translation: report my speeches if you like, but put my talk in print and you shall have the mitten.

A letter from London dated July 3, 1843, introduces the attaché to Edmund Hopkinson of Edgeworth, Gloucestershire. The writer recalls many agreeable hours at Edgeworth and promises it as his first visit on leaving London. His attaché, whose politics match Hopkinson's own, will arrive days earlier. His quirks will need indulgence, the letter warns, but his novelty, quaint sayings, and queer views of England should afford amusement. The first volume's chapters begin with Uncorking a Bottle.
the-battle-of-the-strong-a-romance-of-tw:
Gilbert Parker called his complete romance of two kingdoms a protest and a deliverance. For seven years, he says, he had written of Canada, and editors expected him to stay there. Parker refused to be confined to one field or to repeat his earlier books.

In 1897 he went to the island of Jersey to break free of that pattern. Contents move from an invasion to scenes in France and Jersey across many years. Parker saw new fields in the Channel Islands, Egypt, South Africa, and India. The complete volume joins those Jersey episodes in one long story of two kingdoms.
the-belton-estate:
Anthony Trollope's novel first appeared in the Fortnightly Review in 1865 and in book form the same year. Chapter one concerns what remains of the Amedroz family. The heir proposes to visit his cousins, and Will Belton is introduced in the third heading.

Three headings play on being safe, then not safe, then safe again against love-making. Miss Amedroz visits Perivale, meets Captain Aylmer's promises, and proves too candid by half. Walks in country and London, evil words, and a story from Mrs Askerton follow. Hashed chicken at a railway hotel and at Aylmer Park gives comic weight to a courtship plot ending in possession.
the-bride-of-the-nile-complete:
Georg Ebers wrote The Bride of the Nile, translated from the German by Clara Bell. The work opens with a preface in which Ebers makes two points for the student reader. First, the word Mukaukas is not a name but a title. Arab writers, he says, use it of the stand-ins of the Byzantine Emperor, set against the Moslem power.

On this he follows de Goeje, and holds his own first view. He grants that those who take the author of the Hieroglyphica to be the man of the same name under Theodosius will not grant the date. Suidas, he notes, lists the works of Horapollo the scholar with no word of the Hieroglyphica.
the-burgomaster-s-wife-complete:
Georg Ebers wrote The Burgomaster's Wife, translated from the German by Mary J. Safford. The complete form opens with a dedication to Baroness Sophie von Brandenstein, née Ebers, his father's only sister. Writing from Leipsic on October 30, 1881, Ebers recalls laboring, as her guest seventeen years before, over the material that forms the book's base. Holland was his mother's home, and its history his favorite study.

A fair portion of Holland's glorious history, he says, affords the espalier round which the tendrils of his narrative entwine. Chapter I then opens in the year 1574, with spring arriving in the Netherlands well ahead of its season. Under a blue sky, gnats dance in the sunshine. White butterflies settle on new-opened yellow flowers. Beside a ditch stood a stork, snapping at a fine frog. One gulp, and the merry jumper vanished down its red beak.
the-captain-s-toll-gate: The Captain's Toll-Gate, by Frank R. Stockton, dated 1903 and carrying a memorial sketch of the author by Mrs. Stockton, opens with its table of contents alone. Thirty-seven chapters are headed, among them Olive, Maria Port, Mrs. Easterfield, Olive Pays Toll, Mr. Claude Locker, Locker released on bail, the conflicting serenades, By Proxy, Here We Go! Lovers Three!, and a late assurance that the stock-market is safe. No page of the story is shown.
the-caxtons-a-family-picture-complete:
Edward Bulwer Lytton, Lord Lytton, wrote The Caxtons as a family picture in novel form, and this record holds the complete work. In his preface he warns readers that the plot is slight and the events are few. Most of the tale, he says, could be found in the records of ordinary life.

The one strand with stronger stakes is the fate of Vivian. Lytton calls the book an experiment apart from his earlier work. Humor serves kind characters rather than sharp satire, and man is shown at rest by his own hearth instead of in action abroad. The narrator's own life story links the cast, and the preface names the pull of home on a young man's path as the book's core concern. Household love takes the front place that grand passion holds in most romances.
the-celebrity-complete:
Winston Churchill wrote this novel, and this record holds the complete work, opening with Volume 1, Chapter I. The narrator looks back on a man he has known since boyhood, long before fame found him. The famous man of the tale is Mr. Charles Wrexell Allen, known through most of the book simply as the Celebrity.

In the old days, the narrator saw no sign of genius in his friend. The boy never read him any manuscripts, and showed none of the odd habits fame later brought. The narrator grants that his own plain, unwatching mind may share the blame for missing early promise. The tale then follows fame, society, and love at the resort of Asquith, where the Celebrity's name draws crowds and stirs rivalry.
the-complete-poetical-works-of-percy-bys:
Percy Bysshe Shelley's poetical works appear here in the Oxford Edition, edited with textual notes by Thomas Hutchinson, M.A., and dated 1914. The title page promises materials never before printed in any edition of the poems. Although this record is named for the complete works, the title page in view is marked Volume 1.

Hutchinson's preface defines his method. The edition holds all Shelley's ascertained poems and fragments of verse that had appeared in print. He worked from the editio princeps, the first printing, as the primary textual authority wherever possible. He refused simply to reprint Mrs. Shelley's recension of 1839 or any later editor's text. Instead, the text rests on a fresh collation of the early editions. Where he departs from an original's wording in a material way, the rejected reading stands in a footnote. For Julian and Maddalo he announces a change of authority in a prefatory note.
the-comrade-in-white:
The Rev. W. H. Leathem, M.A., wrote this poem in numbered sections on Christ's presence with soldiers. Section I looks back to the wars of the Cross. Soldiers then, with high courage and hearts that did not quail, saw the vision of the Holy Grail borne from the skies.

The chalice that once held the wine of the Saviour's sacrifice told those fighters that the Master still met his friends in fellowship. Section II turns to the present: Christ has his soldiers now, fighting oppression, tyranny, and wrong. Amid the conflict they trace the Saviour's influence, not through the Grail but through Christ himself. A veil lifts, and face to face they meet the risen Lord. Section III blesses the vision as still present after all the years. Leathem writes devotional verse for wartime readers, joining old crusading imagery to the modern battlefield.
the-confession-of-a-child-of-the-century:
Alfred de Musset's Confession of a Child of the Century stands here complete, fronted by a preface from Henri de Bornier of the French Academy. Bornier treats genius as a trust, not a plaything: it belongs, he argues, to God, to the world, and to readers yet unborn. His essay is at once a life of the poet and a verdict on him.

By thirty, in Bornier's telling, de Musset was spent, chasing lost youth by artificial means. A literary family's zeal had consumed him early. His passion burned out, and his heart burned with it, so the date of the final curtain hardly matters beside the work already done. For all that, Bornier ranks him among the great poets of every age, and first among poets of love. The confession behind the essay is de Musset's own telling of that brief, blazing youth.
the-confessions-of-harry-lorrequer-compl:
Charles James Lever wrote these confessions of an Irish officer, printed at Dublin in 1839, the year given in Roman numerals on the title page. A verse epigraph sets the barracks tone: soldiers talk of pipe-clay, regulation caps, and mortars, curse their quarters, and pray for the route to Cork or Galway. This record holds the complete work.

The contents open with Harry's arrival in Cork, civic festivities, and private theatricals. Detachment duty at the Burton Arms and life at Callonby follow, with love-making and Miss O'Dowd's adventure. Botanical studies get a comic chapter, arguing the natural system against the Linnaean. A puzzle chapter promises a duel, and a priest's supper brings Father Malachi, the coadjutor, Major Jones, and the abbe. A lady's letter, congratulations, and sick leave round out what is present.
the-continental-monthly-vol-1-no-6-june-:
June 1862 brings the sixth number of The Continental Monthly, devoted to literature and national policy. Its lead piece, The Constitution and Slavery, lays out how the free states and the slave states read the nation's founding charter in opposed ways.

The Southern view, as listed here, holds that the Constitution treats slaves strictly as property that may be bought and sold. It claims all territories stand open to slavery, that Congress may not bar slaveholders from them, and that the Union is a compact of sovereign states that a wronged state may leave. The writer notes that the free states reject all of this, and sets out to treat the legal question rather than the morals of slavery.
the-crisis-complete: Winston Churchill's novel The Crisis is shown here through the contents of its whole set, arranged in books and volumes. Book I opens with chapters on origins, Silas Whipple, and Miss Jinny, moving through Bellegarde and a party. Book II brings in Abraham Lincoln, a chapter called The Crisis itself, and Glencoe, then excursions, warnings to the colonel, and signs of the times. Only the title page and this set-wide contents are present here, so the novel's own pages do not appear.
the-disowned-complete:
Edward Bulwer Lytton opens The Disowned under a motto from G. Knight's Limbo: I'll tell you a story if you please to attend. Chapter I sets an evening of a warm day in the May of a year given as 17--. The sun has set, and twilight gathers over still masses of wood flanking one of those green lanes peculiar to England.

Patches of waste land covered with fern and yellow dwarf furze shrink back from the road. Clusters of rushes hum with gnats until the dark swallows every token of life. The first sound is the light, quick step of a youth. It is betrayed by his elastic tread and by a gay carol he keeps starting over: 'Tis merry, 'tis merry, in good green wood, when birds are about and singing. A heavier step overtakes him, and a good-humoured voice gives the salutation of the evening.
the-divine-comedy-by-dante-illustrated-p: Paradise, the third part of Dante Alighieri's Vision, appears in the English verse of the Rev. H. F. Cary, with art by Gustave Doré. Only the title page and a full list of cantos, from canto one through canto thirty-three, are present here. No verse text appears, so the climb through the spheres of heaven can be traced only from that list of cantos.

Purgatory, the second part of Dante Alighieri's Vision, appears in the English verse of the Rev. H. F. Cary, with art by Gustave Doré. A list of all thirty-three cantos opens the volume. Two lines of canto one follow, where the poet's bark of song lifts its sail on better waves. Little more than the title page, the canto list, and those first lines are present here.
the-dwelling-place-of-light-complete:
Winston Churchill's novel The Dwelling-Place of Light, dated 1917, opens in the mill city of Hampton, New England. Edward Bumpus, at fifty-five, keeps the gate of the vast Chippering Mill, torn from his old Yankee ledge like a stone rolled by a glacier. The smoky town, full of new tongues, seems to him a bad dream on his own soil.

His daughter Janet works in the mill office and draws the owner's eye. Labour strife, desire, and old faith clash round her. Churchill, the American novelist, maps a nation changed by mills and migrants.
the-early-life-of-mark-rutherford-w-hale:
The Early Life of Mark Rutherford, printed by Oxford University Press in 1913, prints the notes of W. Hale White, who wrote as Mark Rutherford. His son's foreword tells how the elder White, asked to set down facts for his kin, left the notes to his daughter in his will. She held back, then chose to print them for a wider circle.

White recalls a strict chapel childhood, doubt, and slow self-making. The spare, honest tone matches his famed novels of faith lost and found. Few English lives of the mind read so plain and true.
the-ebb-tide-a-trio-and-quartette:
Robert Louis Stevenson and Lloyd Osbourne wrote The Ebb-Tide together, a tale of the South Seas. Part one opens at night on the beach at Papeete, Tahiti. Round the Pacific, the authors say, white men of all ranks spread trade and disease; some thrive, some rot, and some lack bread in a land of plenty. Three such men sit under a purao tree.

Herrick, Davis, and Huish, broke and shamed, plot to steal a schooner. Stevenson's late tale is bleak where his boy books were bright. Greed and rot, not gold, wait at the end of their cruise.
the-eighteenth-brumaire-of-louis-bonapar: Karl Marx's brilliant 1852 analysis of how Louis Napoleon seized power in France. "History repeats itself, first as tragedy, then as farce": the most quoted line in all of Marx. Witty, savage, and profound, it is political writing at its highest pitch.
the-emperor-complete:
Georg Ebers's The Emperor, in Clara Bell's English rendering, tells of Roman Egypt in Hadrian's day. Ebers's preface says he planned the tale fourteen years back, out of lectures on Rome's rule in Egypt, but set it aside for science. It completes his Egypt set: Uarda for Pharaonic times, An Egyptian Princess for Persian rule, The Sisters for Greek days, and Homo Sum for the desert monks.

Hadrian's visit to Alexandria drives the plot, round the sculptor Pollux, the steward's daughters, and the youth Antinous. Ebers packs the tale with learned, lived detail of the ancient city.
the-expedition-of-the-donner-party-and-i:
Eliza P. Donner Houghton's The Expedition of the Donner Party and Its Tragic Fate tells the tale from inside the family. Contents open with the Pacific Coast in 1845, Senator Benton's speeches, and Frémont's reports, which fired her father George Donner's kin to form the first emigrant party from Illinois to California. Then come the start, the Kansas plains, and letters from her mother on the road.

Fort Laramie, a Fourth of July camp, and Hastings's open letter mark the turn toward ruin. Houghton, a child survivor, writes with care and grief. Her book is a prime first-hand source.
the-forsyte-saga-complete: John Galsworthy wrote The Forsyte Saga, and this complete copy is present here only in front matter and the start of its contents. The contents open with a preface, then The Man of Property in parts. The first heads name an at home at Old Jolyon's, a dinner at Swithin's, plans of a house, and the death of Aunt Ann. No page of the novel itself can be read in this opening portion, so the tale's scenes cannot be stated from this front matter alone.
the-golden-bowl-complete:
Henry James wrote The Golden Bowl. It is dated 1904. This record holds Volumes I and II, complete. Book First is called The Prince. Part First opens in London. The Prince walks there and thinks on the city. He has always liked London when it came to him.

The Prince is a modern Roman. He finds by the Thames a truer image of the old empire than by the Tiber. He drifts into Bond Street. He stops at shop windows full of silver, gold, and jewels. The goods lie tumbled together like loot of far-off wins. His loose gaze and rich tastes mark him at once. He is a man of old name and fine feeling. He is set in a world of costly things, marriages, and money.
the-great-conspiracy-complete:
John Logan wrote The Great Conspiracy: Its Origin and History. This record holds the complete work. His preface sets his aim. He will present authentic facts with historical accuracy. He will be fair in grouping them. He will be true and just in the conclusions drawn. He will not mince words. He seeks favor in no quarter.

Logan traces the conspiracy from its obscure birth. It began in the minds of a few ambitious men in the earliest days of the Republic. It ran through nullification. It reached the bitter and bloody period of armed rebellion. It reaches a still more sinister development of his own day. He worked, he says, from the voluminous records open at the seat of government. He lets the chief actors speak where he can. Conspirators and Union leaders alike get their say.
the-great-war-syndicate:
Frank R. Stockton wrote The Great War Syndicate. Stockton is named as author of The Lady or the Tiger and Rudder Grange. The tale opens in the spring of a year near the close of the nineteenth century. Relations between the United States and Great Britain are strained. The fishing schooner Eliza Drum sails from a port in Maine. She makes for the banks of Newfoundland.

A new system guards the American fishing fleet. United States cruisers stay on the grounds. They warn American craft from the three-mile limit. They watch the British naval vessels. The Eliza Drum works too well at her fishing. She hauls cod at a point two and three-quarter miles, or three and a quarter, from the Canadian coast. The answer depends on the nationality of the calculator. The British cruiser Dog Star seizes her. The American cruiser Lennehaha arrives too late.
the-grounds-of-christianity-examined-by-: George Bethune English wrote The Grounds of Christianity Examined by Comparing the New Testament with the Old. English held the degree A.M. The book was printed at Boston in 1813. Its motto is: First understand, then judge. English dedicates it to the intelligent and the candid. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page, the dedication, and the start of a contents list. The chapters set out the marks of the Messiah given by the Hebrew prophets. They test the character of Jesus by those marks.
the-heart-of-mid-lothian-complete: The complete Heart of Mid-Lothian gathers Jeanie Deans's whole heroic journey — from Edinburgh's Tolbooth to her pilgrimage to London for royal mercy. Scott's most tender and moral novel, in one volume. A masterpiece of the Waverley series. No reader finishes Jeanie's journey unchanged by her quiet, unshakeable goodness.
the-lamp-of-fate: The Lamp of Fate is a novel of destiny and desire. Its characters follow the strange lights that guide their lives. Love and fortune hang in the balance. A romantic tale of fate's turning wheel.
the-landlord-at-lion-s-head-complete:
William Dean Howells explains in a bibliographical note how a Vermont mountain seen from Lake Champlain gave him his title. French pioneers called the peak Le Lion Couchant, while Yankees preferred the Camel Hump name. Howells saw a sleeping lion and named his planned summer hotel novel from that shape.

He wrote the story over about a year and saw it serialized before book publication in 1896. The complete record presents the whole novel about a landlord, his hotel, and the guests whose lives cross there. Howells treats ambition and manners with close, quiet observation.
the-lane-that-had-no-turning-complete: Gilbert Parker gathered his Pontiac tales into a complete set, dedicated to Sir Wilfrid Laurier in a letter recalling work begun in 1892. Only the contents and the start of that dedication are present here, listing the title tale plus stories across four volumes, among them Parpon the Dwarf, Mathurin, and Medallion Whim. The tales themselves do not appear in this record, so readers see the full plan of the collection without its opening story.
the-last-of-the-barons-complete:
Edward Bulwer Lytton prefaces his historical novel with a long letter defending fiction that borrows people from real records. He argues that a tale can fill cold chronicle outlines with color, habit, and motive. Research, he says, should sober the fancy that brings an age to life.

The complete novel turns to England under Edward IV and to Earl Warwick, the great baron known as the Kingmaker. Court intrigue, rebellion, and private love cross through the story. Lytton asks readers to learn how people of that age thought and felt, not just what dates they filled.
the-life-of-napoleon-i-complete: John Holland Rose wrote his life of Napoleon the First with new material from British official records, first published in December 1901. Only the title pages and the start of the contents are present here for the complete work, in a 1910 Bell edition dedicated to Lord Acton. A note on the Republican calendar opens the contents list. Rose motto from Napoleon tells his son to read and reflect on history often. The biography itself is not included in this record.
the-log-of-the-empire-state: Geneve Shaffer keeps the log of a voyage aboard the Empire State — day by day, port by port, with a traveler's eye for people and places. Shipboard life, strange shores, and fellow passengers fill an engaging narrative. A pleasant companion for readers who love the romance of sea travel.
the-papers-and-writings-of-abraham-linco: The complete papers and writings of Abraham Lincoln: every word. Speeches, letters, and state papers. The essential American. History's greatest president, lincoln entire: speeches and letters, the essential American, history's greatest president, speeches and letters.
the-parasite:
Arthur Conan Doyle wrote this tale of mesmerism in 1894, in the years of his Holmes fame. Its theme is the theft of a man's will by the mind of a strong foe. Doyle had read much on hypnotism, the hot theme of the late Victorian years.

A young man of science scoffs at the claim that minds can rule minds at a range. A woman with the gift then takes his will in hand and bends his life to her ends. The tale is the most grim of its age on the dread of lost self rule.
the-people-for-whom-shakespeare-wrote: Charles Dudley Warner's People for Whom Shakespeare Wrote: the Elizabethan audience. The groundlings' world, vividly drawn. Literary history. The groundlings' world revived, elizabethan London, vividly drawn, literary history, the groundlings' world, Elizabethan London, the Elizabethan audience.
the-pirate: The Pirate, Frederick Marryat's novel. The sea rover's tale. This book preserves that adventure. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Tomorrow's readers will find it. Writers of history may cite it later.
the-pit-prop-syndicate: The Pit Prop Syndicate, Freeman Wills Crofts's mystery. The syndicate's scheme. This book preserves that tale. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
the-poetical-works-of-oliver-wendell-hol: The complete Holmes in one volume — from Old Ironsides to the last teacup poems, the whole bright career of Boston's Autocrat. Doctor, wit, and patriot, he was among America's best-loved voices. An essential classic for every American shelf. Here is a lifetime of wit and warmth between two covers.
the-red-lily-complete: The complete Red Lily gathers Anatole France's great novel whole. Therese's story runs from first flirtation to final choice. Parisian irony sparkles at its very finest. The definitive text of a true and lasting masterpiece.
the-wandering-jew-complete: Eugène Sue’s Wandering Jew, the whole great serial in one volume. The Rennepont heirs face the scheming Jesuits. Grand suspense fills every chapter. The bestselling novel of the 1800s, complete at last, melodrama's masterpiece.
the-woman-in-white: Wilkie Collins's 1860 sensation novel, one of the first great mystery thrillers. A young drawing teacher encounters a mysterious woman in white on a midnight road, and is pulled into a plot of switched identities, a sinister Italian count, and a wife imprisoned in an asylum. With its cliffhangers and multiple narrators, it invented the page-turner, and Count Fosco remains one of fiction's great villains.
the-yosemite: John Muir, the great prophet of the wilderness, pours his love for Yosemite into these glowing pages. Granite cliffs, waterfalls, and giant sequoias live in prose that helped save the valley for the nation. The book that made Yosemite a household word.
tom-swift-and-his-electric-locomotive-or: Tom Swift builds a locomotive that runs two miles a minute in this 1922 adventure, then races it against sabotage and storms. High-speed rail thrills from the boy inventor's later years. Speed, danger, and ingenuity on the rails.
trinity-site: This entry documents the Trinity atomic test site. The first bomb. The Tower library holds the full text. It sited Trinity. Desert woke. Fire bloomed. Age dawned. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
woman-in-white: Woman in White, Wilkie Collins's classic. Another edition. This book preserves that novel. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
yvette: Maupassant's Yvette is a polished novella of Parisian life. A young courtesan's daughter faces the world's harsh and judging gaze. The master's cool irony cuts very deep. A small and perfect gem of French realism.
zibeline-complete: The complete Zibeline gathers the French novel whole and uncut. The full arc of its elegant drama slowly unfolds. A polished portrait of a vanished and glittering age. The definitive single-volume text, complete and uncut.
zola-three-cities-complete:
Vizetelly translated Zola's Three Cities whole: Lourdes, Rome, and Paris. The first novel opens on a train packed with pilgrims and patients in third class. They chant the Ave maris Stella as the train leaves the Orleans terminus at dawn.

Marie, feverish on her couch of pain, cries out with joy at the city walls. Her father and Abbe Pierre Froment watch her with fond worry. The ride to Lourdes will take more than twenty-two hours, until past three next morning. Froment, a priest losing his faith, seeks truth in each city in turn, and the set forms Zola's plea for reason and justice.
